Posted May 21, 2002
Analysis by Richard Cowan
See

Tomorrow the Home Affairs Select Committee of the House of Commons will recommend the reclassification of cannabis to make possession a non-arrestable offence. The government will insist that this does not mean that cannabis has been " decriminalized " but the law will no longer serve as a way to intimidate users into silence. That is the only way that prohibition could be maintained.

As a Cuban dissident recently said of the Castro government, " The government is afraid of this liberating gesture, where a social vanguard is showing it has no fear. The government is afraid when the people are not afraid. "

The UK report, which follows a 10-month inquiry, is expected to be highly critical of the Blair government's drugs policies. This means that the UK government will be under pressure to do something, anything, to appear to " get tough " on hard drugs, but " getting tough " on cannabis in the UK is no longer politically possible, much less rewarding.
From October 2000 -- See

Scotland has its own parliament now, and is on its own track.
See

In the larger cities like Manchester, coffee shops will probably be tolerated because the police have too much else to do. The fact that these places tend to become sanctuaries for medical users also inhibits the UK police, many of whom are on our side some because they are also tokers.

The only really sad part of the Stockport story was that Dutch Experience co-founder Colin Davies was held in Strangeways Prison without bail for six months before being released last week.

His trial is scheduled for late June. He has twice been acquitted on charges of supplying cannabis to sick people. It is likely to happen again, and then the Dutch Experience would become a legal precedent as well.
See

In what may be bad news for GW Pharmaceuticals, the UK's National Institute for Clinical Excellence (NICE) -- which is described as " the health economics watchdog " -- has indicated concerns about the " cost effectiveness " of GW's products.

This would mean that the bulk of the medical cannabis market would continue to be filled by growers and coffee shops

Thus, we are not the ones tying medical cannabis to the recreational market. That is the result of governments refusing to take care of the needs of the patients.

Consider where this leaves things in the UK.

More coffee shops will be opened by an ever more defiant community, whose members can no longer be arrested, and medical users will be their most conspicuous patrons. The government's new policy will put it in the position of trying to defend leaving cannabis in the black market. That is an untenable argument.

There will likely be a period in which the UK " goes Dutch " with de facto legalization through the coffee shops. However, unlike The Netherlands, the UK does not have a tradition of formal tolerance of illegal activity. Consequently, the pressure on the UK government to move to amend the UN treaties will grow. Unlike The Netherlands and Switzerland, which think of themselves as too small to challenge the treaties alone, the UK can easily do so. Also the UK cannot be readily pressured by DEAland, because the Bush administration needs Blair's support in the terror war.

When the UK goes, the way will be clear for the rest of the Commonwealth, and that is the end of cannabis prohibition in the civilized world. At that point the pressure on DEAland will be enormous, assuming that DEAland's prohibitionist media ever report that the world is round.

The government is afraid when the people are not afraid.

Remember that!
